findings.title: Land and sea offer no fixed refuge
findings.claim: Across 17:68-69, the repeated security challenge moves from sinking ground and a stone-bearing wind to another sea entry and a ship-breaking wind. The sequence makes neither land nor sea an autonomous refuge; its final drowning and absent claimant extend exposure from the physical setting into recourse.
findings.mechanism: The focus security question and return into the sea meet 17:68's matching security question, sinking side, and projectile wind. The prior sea passage in 17:66 supplies the setting that the focus re-enters. Repeated dispatch and destructive outcomes make relocation itself fail as protection; the focus's no-claimant close carries that failure into the legal relation.
findings.reader_payoff: A reader can see why the change of medium is not a guarantee: the sea passage is itself a gift of carriage and mercy, while the neighboring warning exposes both land and sea to reversal.
findings.containment: The focus still describes a possible return to the sea followed by wind and drowning. This is a reading of the paired warnings, not a claim that land and sea are identical or that every passage is unsafe. The sound branch is an image-level echo of a loud storm, not an assertion that thunder is named. A live alternative treats the two warnings as adjacent dangers without the broader no-refuge pattern.

findings.mechanism: At 17:66, gentle propulsion and mercy frame the vessel as provision; 17:67 supplies rescue followed by turning away; the focus attaches the later drowning to denial through its causal phrase. The following 17:70 names carrying and honor again, so the focus storm reverses the transport relation without erasing the gift or human dignity.

The reading does not say that every voyage reverses, that mercy has been withdrawn generally, or that human honor is denied. A live alternative gives denial its broader rejection sense without foregrounding ingratitude.

findings.title: Following and claiming face opposite directions
findings.claim: The pericope first names people who choose to follow the tempter and receive a full recompense; the focus later says no claimant can be found against God concerning the threatened event. The same supplied word family therefore moves from following an authority to pursuing a counterclaim, while the liability of the first relation remains attached.
findings.mechanism: The context carrier at 17:63 is the person who follows, and its recompense and full measure make that following answerable. The focus carrier names a rights-pursuer under negation. Their contact reverses the direction of pursuit: consequence follows the chosen allegiance, while no claimant follows up a demand against God.
findings.reader_payoff: The closing absence is newly legible beside the earlier following: the pericope allows a consequence to adhere to a person's allegiance while denying a reverse claim against God.
findings.containment: The focus noun remains a claimant or rights-pursuer in its immediate legal clause. The liability facet is an attributed root-family echo, not a claim that the focus noun literally means an abstract liability. A live alternative keeps the two uses independent.

Context at 17:62 names the Day and resurrection, 17:71 names the Day of assembly, and 17:72 names the later realm. The focus's other-time word also meets the later-realm occurrence at 17:72, allowing immediate maritime repetition and ultimate return to coexist.
findings.reader_payoff: The return reads as a second exposure situated inside a pericope that already names final return and reckoning, rather than as a random repetition alone.
findings.containment: The focus syntax directly describes returning the people to the sea another time. No schedule, regular interval, or resurrection statement is asserted by this ayah. The afterlife and destination facets remain contextual echoes, and the 17:64 HFT root mapping is excluded because its mapped root does not match the supplied context root.
